---
title: "What must be new at prediction time"
---

The earlier page on [populations and samples](../statistical-inference/populations-and-samples.qmd) required an inferential claim to specify the population represented by a sample. Predictive evaluation requires a related decision. We must say which responses were unavailable during fitting and what information is available when those responses are predicted. This is the [prediction-unit problem](index.qmd) in operational form.

[**Out-of-sample prediction**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-cv.html) predicts responses that did not contribute to fitting the model. This definition leaves an important question open: is the held-out response new only as a row, or is its reader or text also absent from training?

## Natural Stories

We use the corrected [Natural Stories release](https://github.com/languageMIT/naturalstories/tree/4700daad696e942f5aba23c957a7423d0de66612), introduced and validated by [Futrell et al. (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10579-020-09503-7), throughout the first six pages of this unit. The corpus contains English stories enriched for low-frequency syntactic constructions, self-paced reading times, and aligned lexical annotations. The corrected release fixes a one-position displacement in the reading-time records. Its preprocessing excludes reader-story passes with fewer than five correct comprehension answers and reading times outside the release's 100-to-3,000-ms window.

The code below constructs the prediction table from the tracked release. One row is one retained button latency for one reader at one word position. It is a self-paced reading time, not an eye fixation.

```{r}
#| label: natural-targets
#| message: false
#| warning: false

natural_all <- readRDS(
  "data/natural-stories/natural-stories-corrected.rds"
)
natural_all$row_id <- seq_len(nrow(natural_all))

complete_prediction_row <- with(
  natural_all,
  is.finite(log_rt) & is.finite(word_length) &
    is.finite(log_unigram_frequency) & is.finite(gpt3_surprisal)
)

natural <- natural_all[complete_prediction_row, c(
  "row_id", "participant_id", "story_id", "sentence_id",
  "word_position", "word", "word_length", "log_rt",
  "log_unigram_frequency", "gpt3_surprisal"
)]
natural$position_id <- paste(
  natural$story_id, natural$word_position, sep = ":"
)

target_inventory <- data.frame(
  object = c(
    "retained response row", "participant", "story", "sentence",
    "story-position", "participant-story pass"
  ),
  count = c(
    nrow(natural),
    length(unique(natural$participant_id)),
    length(unique(natural$story_id)),
    length(unique(natural$sentence_id)),
    length(unique(natural$position_id)),
    length(unique(paste(
      natural$participant_id, natural$story_id, sep = ":"
    )))
  )
)

participant_means <- aggregate(
  log_rt ~ participant_id, data = natural, FUN = mean
)
names(participant_means) <- c("group_id", "mean_log_rt")
participant_means$unit <- "Participant"

story_means <- aggregate(
  log_rt ~ story_id, data = natural, FUN = mean
)
names(story_means) <- c("group_id", "mean_log_rt")
story_means$unit <- "Story"

target_variation <- rbind(participant_means, story_means)
target_variation$rank_within_unit <- ave(
  target_variation$mean_log_rt,
  target_variation$unit,
  FUN = function(x) rank(x, ties.method = "first")
)

target_inventory

ggplot2::ggplot(
  target_variation,
  ggplot2::aes(rank_within_unit, mean_log_rt)
) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 1.2, alpha = 0.7, color = "grey25") + # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ unit, scales = "free_x") +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Group rank by mean response",
    y = "Mean log reading time"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_classic(base_size = 11)
```

The prepared release has `r format(nrow(natural_all), big.mark = ",")` response rows from `r length(unique(natural_all$participant_id))` participants and `r length(unique(natural_all$story_id))` stories. Requiring finite word length, log unigram frequency, and GPT-3 surprisal retains `r format(nrow(natural), big.mark = ",")` rows at `r format(length(unique(natural$position_id)), big.mark = ",")` contextual word positions. The figure shows why a response row, participant, and story are not interchangeable units: the participant and story means vary, but there are only `r nrow(story_means)` story-level values.

## Three prediction targets

All three procedures used later fit the population regression

$$
\log RT_i
=
\beta_0+\beta_1z(L_i)+\beta_2z(F_i)+\beta_3z(S_i)+\epsilon_i,
$$

where $L_i$ is word length, $F_i$ is log unigram frequency, and $S_i$ is released GPT-3 surprisal. What changes is the **prediction unit**, the object excluded from training.

| target | absent from fitting | still represented in fitting |
|:--|:--|:--|
| new response row | that latency | the reader and story |
| new participant | every latency from that reader | the ten stories |
| omitted enriched story | every latency from that story | the reader population represented by the other stories |

These separations ask different questions. A random row split evaluates another response from the represented collection of readers and stories. A participant split evaluates a reader absent from fitting. A story split evaluates one omitted member of these deliberately enriched texts.

The story target needs especially narrow wording. The corpus supplies `r nrow(story_means)` opportunities to inspect an omitted story, not `r format(nrow(natural), big.mark = ",")` independent story transfers. Leave-one-story-out results consequently describe these ten omissions; they do not estimate performance for an unrestricted population of English texts.

## The prediction information set

Holding out a group does not by itself determine which information about it may be used. In these analyses, a held-out row keeps its word length, frequency, and surprisal because those predictors are available at prediction time. A held-out participant contributes no reading-time response to fitting. A held-out story contributes its lexical predictors but no response from any of its positions.

The preprocessing rule is part of the information set. Each predictor mean and standard deviation is estimated from training rows and then applied to test rows. A full-data center would let held-out predictor values affect the training representation. A separately estimated test center would place the test observations in a different coordinate system.

## Theory determines what should be held out

The most demanding split is not automatically the right one. A reading model used for an already represented reader may reasonably target another response row. A claim about transfer across readers requires participant folds. A claim about connected text requires story folds and enough story-level replication to support it.

Successful prediction also does not establish a processing mechanism. Word surprisal can improve a held-out score without showing that readers internally represent the fitted language model's probabilities. Predictive evaluation establishes performance for a stated response, information set, split, and population; the mechanism requires additional evidence.

## Checking the target

1. Which Natural Stories target keeps the same reader and story represented during fitting?
2. What must move together when the target is a reader absent during fitting?
3. Why do the retained response rows not provide that many independent evaluations of an omitted story?
4. Which predictor transformations must be estimated without the held-out responses?

Out-of-sample prediction requires a response excluded from fitting. A complete predictive question also states which groups are held out, which predictors remain available, and where the result should generalize. The [previous page](index.qmd) introduces this sequence; the [next page](training-and-test-data.qmd) implements one participant-held-out split and makes its training-only preprocessing visible.
